doc.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000

title: What Hamilton is doing in 2000, and why he dislikes the word jazz
summary: Opening of the interview; he describes his orchestra, tours and recordings, and argues music should be called by its maker's name.

story.theme_name: Opening the interview: Monk Rowe's welcome and archive boilerplate
story.community_name: Opening the Hamilton College interview: introductions and boilerplate

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe and we’re filming in Manhattan today, and I’m very, very pleased to have Chico Hamilton with me, who has had a long, illustrious and varied career in music. Would you mind telling me what you’re up to in the year 2000?

Sure. I’m just trying to stay alive. No, as a matter of fact we’re up to a whole lot of things. The group, my orchestra — I don’t refer to it as a band, it’s an orchestra, because I think we try to cover all facets of music, not just one direction you know, and not just necessarily under the terminology of even jazz — J-A-Z-Z. I really disapprove of the word myself. I’m in complete accordance with people, with Duke Ellington, Miles Davis, people like that. Why not call it just my music, Chico’s music? Duke Ellington’s music, Duke Ellington’s music. Miles Davis’ music, Miles’ music. Benny Goodman, Benny Goodman’s music. Why label it jazz? Because the word itself has nothing to do with music, from the origin. But anyway, getting back to the two thou, we have tours lined up, European, the Far East, more recordings, and that’s about the size of it. You know you can’t do any more than that.
Right. Does it make a problem, if you’re trying to find a record label to promote your work, they need to put a title to what it is? If you don’t want to call it jazz but they do?

Why not just call it music? You know? That’s what it is. Because basically, primarily, all we’re dealing in is human emotions, is the way one might feel. And I don’t expect you to feel the same way that I do about a note or a sound. And it’s good because you don’t feel the same way because that way we have an abundance of a variety of emotions. Everybody puts their feelings into a mood and it becomes different, which is dynamite. Because if it all sounds the same it would be boring as hell as far as I was concerned. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
